1:
The chapter's very opening sentence, the witnesses note, is fashioned to instruct rather than merely to date. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fasten on its didactic and rhetorical cast: in place of the precise chronological notice of 2 Kings 18:13, the Chronicler sets down the loose formula "after these things, and the establishment thereof" — after these events and this fidelity, echoing 2 Chronicles 31:20 — and then Sennacherib comes, enters Judah, encamps against the fenced cities, and thinks to break them open for himself. He had already taken many and pushed as far as Lachish in the south-west before he turned toward Jerusalem. The reformed John Gill fixes the moment: it fell in the fourteenth year of the reign, when religion and the temple service were well settled, Hezekiah firm on his throne, the Philistines beaten and the Assyrian yoke cast off, the kingdom prosperous.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott gives the enemy his true name — the monuments' Sin-ahi-iriba — and renders the last clause "said to himself that he would break them open." Kings adds that he succeeded, taking all the fenced cities; Sennacherib's own inscription boasts of forty-six strong cities captured. Here Ellicott exposes the Chronicler's method: his object is to relate the mighty deliverance, and so he omits whatever would weaken that impression — above all Hezekiah's submission and payment of tribute recorded at 2 Kings 18:14, which Isaiah too passes over. Why the omission? A quiet difference opens. Keil holds the negotiations had no bearing on the war's after-course; Thenius, as reported by Ellicott, alleged the Chronicler was unwilling to name Hezekiah's forced sacrilege — a charge Ellicott sets aside in favour of Keil's simpler reason and the writer's manifest aim.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs the providence. Sennacherib, the terror and scourge of that world as Nebuchadnezzar would later be, aimed at universal empire on the ruins of his neighbours; his predecessor Shalmaneser had swallowed the ten tribes, and he thought to win Judah the same way. Yet Henry finds God's ordering everywhere: the blow fell only after the reformation was finished and established, lest it be stopped; perhaps to chastise Hezekiah, whom the idolater reckoned profane for pulling down the altars; and chiefly that God might show himself strong for a returning, reforming people and take to himself the honour of their rescue. The wesleyan-arminian witnesses seal the point: Adam Clarke observes that God did not suffer this pious prince to be disturbed till his reformation was complete, and John Wesley reads the emphatic preface as teaching that we may be in the way of our duty, and yet meet with trouble and danger, permitted for the trial of our confidence and the proof of God's care.
2:
Hezekiah's alertness is the note the witnesses first sound: he saw what was coming and moved before it arrived. The reformed John Gill takes the seeing for a reading of the reports that reached him — he perceived by the taking of the fenced cities in the enemy's path that Sennacherib meant to besiege and, if he could, storm Jerusalem. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens the Hebrew: "his face was for the war," his whole purpose set toward it, as at 2 Chronicles 20:3.

The defensive works now begun are, Keil and Delitzsch observe, reported in neither 2 Kings 18 nor Isaiah 36, yet stand confirmed by Isaiah 22:8-11 and by the notice of the conduit at 2 Kings 20:20, which the chapter itself will echo at v.30. Hezekiah takes counsel with his princes and warriors to cover the waters of the springs outside the city; the verb, this grammatical-historical pair insist, does not mean to obstruct but to hide — to roof the springs over and lead their water by underground channels, drying up the brook (the Gihon) that the overflow had formed. Ellicott adds that "to stop" is to close in with masonry so as to conceal, and that the princes helped him precisely by gathering much people to the labour of the next verse.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke supplies from the parallel what the Chronicler suppresses: this was the fourteenth year, and Hezekiah at first bought the invader off with three hundred talents of silver and thirty of gold, emptying his own treasuries and even stripping the house of the Lord to satisfy the Assyrian's avarice, as 2 Kings 18:13 and following relate. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry frames the whole double policy the verses will unfold: with his princes' advice Hezekiah resolved that the country should give the invader a cold reception and the city a warm one — the fields robbed of water, the walls made strong. The witnesses do not divide; they show a king who, seeing the storm, neither despairs nor merely negotiates, but turns at once to the sober work of defence, provoking the enemy's thirst while he braces his own gates. Keil and Delitzsch make it a mark of their method that a work unmentioned in Kings and in Isaiah's own narrative is yet vouched for by the prophet's oracle and by the later notice of the conduit, so that the Chronicler recovers a true memory of the siege rather than inventing one; and Ellicott's nicety over the two Hebrew words for spring and fountain shows the same close attention. What all the witnesses press is that Hezekiah's faith was never idle — the king who would soon cry to heaven first set his princes and people to the spade, judging that to trust God and to labour were not two things but one.
3:
The council of war is the verse's substance, and the witnesses attend to both its deliberation and its first stratagem. The reformed John Gill reads it plainly: Hezekiah consulted his nobles and the officers of his army what steps should be taken to resist, retard, and distress the enemy, and among the measures proposed was the stopping of the springs. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch take the verse together with those that follow: the king showed himself strong, as the same verb is used at 2 Chronicles 15:8 and 2 Chronicles 23:1, gathering much people who covered every fountain and the brook that ran through the land — the Gihon — with the reasoning the text gives in its own mouth: "Why should the kings of Assyria come, and find much water?"

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws out the second half of the design, which the bare verb of stopping conceals: the waters were not only hidden from the foe but withal drawn by secret pipes underground into Jerusalem, so that the same stroke that starved the besiegers of drink supplied the besieged. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry expands the military wisdom of it. A powerful army, wanting water but a few days, becomes a heap of dry dust; and so all hands were set to stop the fountains and turn the brook into the city by conduits under the ground — the very policy, Henry notes, commonly practised in his own day of destroying the forage before an invading army.

The witnesses do not contend. Gill fixes the counsel, Keil the courage and the labour, Wesley the ingenious diverting of the water inward, Henry the strategy of a scorched approach. Between them they show a king who trusts God and yet leaves nothing to chance, taking the plainest of measures — denying the enemy the one thing an army in an arid land cannot do without — while quietly securing his own people's supply. It is prudence and faith joined in a single act; the God who would presently strike the Assyrian by an angel is first served by pick and spade, and Hezekiah's confidence expresses itself not in idleness but in the diligent stopping of every spring outside the wall, that the invader might find the goodly land turned, at his coming, into a waterless waste. And Keil marks how the workmen speak the theology in their own mouths: they laboured, the text says, that the kings of Assyria might not come and find much water — a homely confession that even the plainest defensive measure was undertaken with an eye to the enemy God would presently rout. The stopping of the springs is thus at once strategy and testimony, the act of a people who reckoned the coming host already doomed.
4:
The great labour of stopping the water is now carried through by the assembled multitude, and the witnesses gather around its wisdom. The reformed John Gill notes only that the much people were gathered at the instance of Hezekiah and his officers; the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke supplies the sense of it. It was prudently done, for without water how could an immense army subsist in an arid country? The Assyrian host, he judges, suffered much from the want; and he reaches for a Christian parallel eighteen centuries later, when the crusaders came up against Jerusalem in 1099 and the people of the city stopped the wells, so that the besieging army was reduced to the greatest distress.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott brings his customary care to the vocabulary. The fountains here are named by one Hebrew word where the previous verse had another for springs; the brook is the wady, the Gihon that flowed through the valley of Hinnom, fed by the very springs Hezekiah was closing; and "that ran" he renders "that was flowing over," as at Isaiah 8:8, so that the stream was simply the overflow of the springs, which now failed at their source. The phrase "the kings of Assyria," he adds, is a vague rhetorical plural like that at 2 Chronicles 28:16; and he recalls that the son of Sirach remembered this very work, that Hezekiah fortified his city and brought water into the midst of it.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry had already read the whole enterprise as a lesson in trusting God without tempting him. The country was made to give the enemy a cold reception, that his army, wanting water, might perish or at least be weakened and unfit for service; and the spade set to the springs is, in Henry's hands, an emblem of the truth that those who trust God with their safety must yet use proper means, else they tempt him — God will provide, but so must we also. The witnesses do not divide; Gill fixes the fact, Clarke its prudence and its later echo, Ellicott its exact terms, Henry its lesson. Together they show a whole people digging in faith, denying the invader the water of the land while their king waits upon the God who alone can save. And the witnesses let the labour preach: what looked like mere engineering was, in Henry's hands, an act of faith, and in Clarke's a proof that God's people are to be as prudent as they are believing. The son of Sirach's later memory of the work, which Ellicott recovers, shows that the deed was remembered in Israel long after as a mark of Hezekiah's wisdom; and the whole scene stands as a rebuke both to the sloth that will not use means and to the presumption that trusts in means alone.
5:
With the fields made barren the king turns to the walls, and the verse crowds together a whole programme of fortification. The reformed John Gill hears the opening words theologically: Hezekiah strengthened himself first of all in the Lord his God, and then set his city in the best posture of defence he could. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott unfolds the several works with the philologist's exactness. "He took courage," as the same verb is used at 2 Chronicles 15:8; he built up all the wall that was broken — the many breaches of Isaiah 22:9-10, where houses were pulled down to fortify it; he built another wall without, the rampart enclosing the lower city, the two walls of Isaiah 22:11; he repaired Millo, the rampart of the city of David; and he made missiles and shields in abundance.

Over one clause the text is genuinely obscure, and Ellicott lays the options out. The Hebrew as pointed reads "and went up upon the towers," which yields no good sense; a different division of the letters gives "and raised upon it towers," which he thinks probably right, while Thenius, as reported by Ellicott, would keep the received reading and understand it of heightening towers the wall already possessed, since 2 Chronicles 26:9 shows towers there before. The versions wander — the Septuagint gives simply "and towers," the Vulgate "and he built towers thereon" — a sure sign the phrase was felt to be hard.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the whole into his standing maxim. Hezekiah repaired the wall, raised the towers, made darts and shields, and appointed captains; and in all this he was giving the city a warm reception to answer the country's cold one. Yet the works of the hand do not, in Henry's reading, displace the trust of the heart: those that trust God with their safety must yet use proper means for their safety, otherwise they tempt him, and do not trust him — God will provide, but so must we also. The witnesses do not divide. Gill grounds the strengthening in God, Ellicott secures the masonry and its disputed clause, Henry weds the means to the faith. Between them they show a Jerusalem walled, towered, and armed, made ready by every human art precisely because its king had first strengthened himself in the LORD. And the witnesses let the crowded verse speak its own lesson: a king may repair walls, raise towers, and forge weapons without any slackening of trust, so long as he strengthens himself first, as Gill insists, in the Lord his God. The masonry and the faith are not rivals but a single obedience; and even the obscure clause over the towers, on which Ellicott and Thenius differ, leaves untouched the plain sense that Jerusalem was made, by every art at the king's command, ready to endure a siege.
6:
The last of the preparations is the raising of officers and the rallying of the people, and the witnesses move from the muster to the morale. The reformed John Gill notes that the captains of war were set over the people to teach them the exercises of war, to lead them against the enemy, and to direct them in the defence of the city. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch add that Hezekiah then gathered the populace of Jerusalem into the open space at the city gate — which gate is not told, as with the assembly at Nehemiah 8:1 — and addressed them with encouraging words, as he had done to the Levites at 2 Chronicles 30:22. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fixes the peculiar idiom "captains of war," literally "captains of battles," a phrase found here only, and takes the street for the broad open place before the gate, where the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke observes the people were wont to gather for judgment.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry enters into the temper of the scene. Hezekiah was himself undaunted, confident the invasion would issue well, and out of that confidence he spoke to the heart of his people and especially of his captains, putting life into them. Henry draws the contrast that gives the moment its weight: the king was not like his father Ahaz, who had much guilt to terrify him and no faith to encourage him, so that in a time of public danger his heart was moved as the trees of the wood are moved with the wind, and the heart of his people with it, as Isaiah 7:2 records. The son's steadiness steadies the city.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Keil fix the appointing of officers and the gathering at the gate; Ellicott and Clarke the terms and the place; Henry the courage that a believing king communicates to a frightened people. Between them they show that the final and best of Hezekiah's defences was neither wall nor weapon but a word — a king standing in the open place of his threatened city and speaking comfort, not out of bravado but out of faith, so that the people might lean, as the next verses will show, upon what he said. The captains marshal the men; the king marshals their hearts. And the witnesses let the gathering at the gate carry its weight: a king who had stopped the springs and armed the walls knew that neither could hold a city whose heart had failed, and so he came down among his people to speak to that heart. The contrast with Ahaz, which Henry presses, is the contrast of two reigns — the one shaken like a leaf for want of faith, the other steady because its faith was sure; and the people, watching their king unafraid, took courage from his courage.
7:
The king's charge itself now begins, and it is built, the witnesses observe, out of the older words of Scripture. The reformed John Gill glosses the opening simply — be of good heart and spirit, and quit yourselves like men. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott traces the phrases to their sources: "be strong and courageous, be not afraid nor dismayed" echoes both the charge of Deuteronomy 31:6 and Jehoshaphat's word before battle at 2 Chronicles 20:15, "be not afraid nor dismayed for this great multitude"; and "there be more with us than with him" is a plain reminiscence of Elisha's assurance at 2 Kings 6:16. Ellicott adds the historian's caution that we need not suppose the Chronicler professes to give the exact words of the exhortation, but only its substance and spirit.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke seizes on that same borrowed sentence — "there be more with us than with him" — as Elisha's, and notes how swiftly its truth was proved by the slaughter the angel would make in the Assyrian camp. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the count as deliberately general, "with us is more," its meaning made precise only in the verse following, where the "more" is named as the LORD himself against a mere arm of flesh.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in the charge the king's first labour, the keeping down of fear. Be strong and courageous, Hezekiah bids them — do not think of surrendering the city, nor of losing it, nor of falling into the enemy's hand; there is no danger. The very encouragement, Henry notes, the prophet had already given from God at Isaiah 10:24, "be not afraid of the Assyrian"; and now the king gives it from the prophet. It was then that the sinners in Zion were afraid, as Isaiah 33:14 says, while the righteous dwelt on high and, meditating on the terror, so conquered it. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the plain sense, Ellicott and Keil the scriptural texture and the general force, Clarke the borrowed confidence soon vindicated, Henry the suppression of fear that faith works. Between them they show a king preaching courage not from temperament but from the promises, arming his people's minds with the very words by which God had armed Israel before. And the witnesses let the borrowed words carry their own comfort: Hezekiah did not invent a new confidence but drew on the old, setting before his people the very promises by which Moses had strengthened Joshua, Jehoshaphat his army, and Elisha his frightened servant. The reformed and grammatical-historical readings meet here — Gill on the plain courage, Ellicott and Keil on its scriptural texture — while Henry and Clarke show how swiftly the promise would be proved, when the more that was with Judah struck down in a night the multitude that was with Assyria.
8:
The ground of all the courage is now laid bare in a single antithesis — an arm of flesh against the living God — and the witnesses dwell on the contrast. The reformed John Gill puts it curtly: with Sennacherib are only weak, frail, mortal men, not at all to be feared, nothing at all in comparison of the Lord. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott shows how the phrase is woven of prophetic threads. "An arm of flesh" recalls the curse on the man that maketh flesh his arm at Jeremiah 17:5, and the taunt of Isaiah 31:3 that the Egyptians' horses are flesh and not spirit; the enemy's power is human, ours superhuman. "To fight our battles" borrows the people's old cry for a king at 1 Samuel 8:20; and "the people rested themselves upon" his words means, literally, that they leaned on them as a man leans on a staff, and so trusted, the very posture named at Isaiah 48:2.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes the verse the king's second labour, the building up of faith to silence fear. Sennacherib has a multitude with him, Hezekiah reasons, and yet there are more with us than with him, for we have God with us, and how many do you reckon him for? With the enemy is an arm of flesh, which he trusts; with us is the LORD, whose power is irresistible and whose promise is inviolable, a God in covenant not merely to help us fight but to fight our battles for us — and so, Henry notes, he did. From this Henry draws his rule: a believing confidence in God will raise us above the prevailing fear of man, for he that feareth the fury of the oppressor forgetteth the LORD his Maker, as Isaiah 51:12-13 charges; and the soldiers of Christ may boldly say, since God is for us, who can be against us, in the confidence of Romans 8:31.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill weighs the two sides — frail flesh against the incomparable Lord; Ellicott traces the antithesis to its prophetic sources and marks the people's trustful leaning; Henry turns it into a doctrine of faith conquering fear. And the last clause, the witnesses agree, is the verse's fruit: the people rested on the king's words — not on his eloquence, but on the God whose covenant help those words proclaimed, so that the whole city was steadied upon a single true sentence, that with them was one greater than all the host of Assyria.
9:
The scene shifts from the walls of Jerusalem to the camp before Lachish, from which Sennacherib sends his envoys, and the witnesses set the parenthesis in its place. The reformed John Gill and the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke both mark what the Chronicler has passed over: the embassy came after Hezekiah had bought the invader off with silver and gold and Sennacherib had for the moment withdrawn, only to send Rabshakeh back with a blasphemous message. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch observe how briefly the whole episode is told beside the long account of 2 Kings 18:17-36: the Chronicler names neither the Assyrian generals nor Hezekiah's ambassadors nor the place of the parley, saying only that his servants were sent while the king himself lay against Lachish with all his power.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds both a textual and an archaeological note. A verb has perhaps dropped from the clause about Lachish, and another from "all his power," which is literally "his dominion" or realm. Sennacherib's great inscription says nothing of the siege of Lachish, but a bas-relief now in the British Museum shows him enthroned before the city, receiving its spoil, with the legend that the king caused the spoils of the city of Lachish to pass before him — the stone confirming the very campaign the verse assumes.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, opening his long meditation on the whole story, reads the embassy as the impiety and malice of the church's enemies. Sennacherib had his hands full at Lachish, yet, hearing that Hezekiah was fortifying Jerusalem and heartening his people, he sent messengers to make speeches and wrote letters to frighten the city into surrender. His malice against the king of Judah, Henry says, showed in his very method: he would not treat with Hezekiah as a man of honour, but used mean and base artifices unbecoming a crowned head, labouring to withdraw the common people from their allegiance and to persuade them to desert their king. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Clarke recover the tribute the Chronicler omits; Keil marks the studied brevity; Ellicott secures the text and the monument; Henry exposes the malice. Between them they show the invader, master of the field, stooping to a war of words against a walled city — the first move of a campaign that the God of Jerusalem would answer not with words but with an angel.
10:
The Assyrian speech opens with a sneer at Judah's confidence — "whereon do ye trust?" — and the witnesses read it as the first assault upon the city's faith. The reformed John Gill hears the taunt at its widest: on what power, in heaven or on earth, do you presume to hold out? The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders it more pointedly, "whereon are ye trusting, and why are ye sitting in distress in Jerusalem?" — the phrase for sitting in distress being that of Jeremiah 10:17 — and notes that these verses reproduce in brief the leading ideas of the long harangue at 2 Kings 18:19-25.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch trace the strategy of the address: only its main ideas are reported, an attempt to shake the people's trust first in Hezekiah and then in God. Why sit ye in the siege, it demands; and the following verse will charge that Hezekiah, in bidding them trust the LORD, is in truth seducing them to death by famine and thirst — a thought expressed even more coarsely in the parallel at 2 Kings 18:27. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, for the fuller detail, simply refers the reader to that same passage in Kings.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the whole speech within the enemy's design against the people's faith. This, he says, was Satan's own aim in every such assault — to destroy men's confidence in God's all-sufficiency, knowing that he gains his point if he can do that, and that we keep our ground only if our faith fail not, as the Lord prayed for Peter at Luke 22:32. The Assyrian would take the city by first weakening the hands that must defend it, teaching the defenders to say, as David's enemies said of him, there is no help for him in God, the very slander of Psalms 3:2. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Ellicott fix the taunt and its scorn, Keil the calculated undermining of trust, Henry the deeper spiritual war beneath the political one. Between them they show that the true target of Sennacherib's rhetoric was not the wall of Jerusalem but the faith of those who manned it. And the witnesses let the sneer expose the strategy behind it: the envoy does not begin with threats of force but with a question meant to unsettle, prying at the seam where confidence meets fear. Gill hears its scope, Ellicott its scorn, Keil its calculation, Henry the spiritual war it opens; and all agree that a taunt aimed at the people's trust is a shrewder weapon than any battering-ram, for a city that keeps its faith is not yet taken, however hard it is pressed, while a city that loses it is taken already. The whole art of the Rabshakeh was to make the defenders their own betrayers.
11:
The envoy turns Hezekiah's own counsel of faith into a charge of cruelty — the king, he says, is luring you to die of hunger and thirst — and the witnesses expose the malice of the twist. The reformed John Gill states the insinuation baldly: Hezekiah, by bidding you hold out on the promise that the LORD will deliver, is in effect handing you over to famine and thirst, for surrender is your only safety. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens the verb — "is not Hezekiah inciting you" — the same word that returns at v.15, and marks how the Chronicler has softened the coarse threat of the parallel at 2 Kings 18:27. He notes too that the boast of cutting off an enemy's water was a stock piece of Assyrian menace, Esarhaddon himself recording of a siege that food and water, the life of their souls, he cut off.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the sentence as one move in the calculated effort to loosen the people's trust: Hezekiah seduces you, the envoy says, to give you over to death by hunger and thirst with his talk of the LORD your God delivering you out of the king of Assyria's hand. The very promise that was the city's comfort is turned into the bait of a trap.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the slander among the base artifices by which Sennacherib sought to detach a people from their king. He represented Hezekiah, Henry says, as one who designed to deceive his subjects into their ruin and to betray them to famine and thirst — the reformer painted as a murderer of his own. The cruelty of the charge lay in its plausibility: a besieged city does hunger, and the tempter had only to name the fear the people already felt and lay it at their king's door. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the insinuation, Ellicott its wording and its Assyrian pedigree, Keil its place in the campaign against faith, Henry its calculated malice. Between them they show the enemy's oldest device — to make the voice of faith sound like the voice of folly, and the shepherd who would save his flock appear as the one who leads them to their death. And the witnesses let the slander show its craft: it fastened on a real hardship — the hunger and thirst of a siege — and turned it against the one man labouring to prevent it, so that the people's very sufferings might be read as their king's design. Gill, Ellicott, Keil, and Henry converge on the perversity of it, that the promise of divine deliverance was made to sound like a sentence of death; and they leave the reader to see that the tempter's surest lie is the one that wears the face of a friendly warning, offering surrender as the only mercy while calling faith a cruelty.
12:
Now the envoy plays his subtlest card, turning Hezekiah's reformation itself into an offence against the very God he trusts. The reformed John Gill, who treats this verse with the three that follow as a single argument, lets the taunt stand: has not Hezekiah taken away the LORD's own high places and altars, and confined all worship to one? The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the charge exactly — "before one altar shall ye worship, and thereon shall ye burn incense" — and observes, comparing 2 Kings 18:22, that the Chronicler is even more emphatic than the older account in asserting the sole validity of the one brazen altar in the temple court. The Assyrian, that is, cynically appeals to the scattered shrines Hezekiah had pulled down, pretending that their removal must have angered the God whose worship they professed to serve.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the verse as the pivot of the whole speech: having questioned the people's trust in Hezekiah, the envoy now aims at their trust in God, insinuating that the king's very piety has stripped them of the many altars that might have propitiated heaven, and left them but one. The taunt is built on a heathen premise — that more altars mean more favour — which mistakes the reforming zeal of Hezekiah for impiety.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry names the slander for what it is. Sennacherib represented Hezekiah, he says, as one who had done his people great wrong and exposed them to the divine displeasure by taking away the high places and altars — as though the destruction of idolatry were the provoking of God rather than the pleasing of him. The witnesses do not divide. Gill bundles the charge with its fellows, Ellicott secures its wording and the Chronicler's emphasis on the single altar, Keil sets it in the campaign against faith, Henry exposes its perversity. Between them they show the enemy at his most insidious, quoting a man's obedience against him and dressing up reformation as sacrilege — the oldest trick of the accuser, to make the fear of God look like the cause of ruin. And the witnesses let the irony stand in full light: the very act that had most pleased God — the purging of the high places — is here paraded as the surest proof of his displeasure, so that the reformer is condemned out of his own reformation. Gill, Ellicott, Keil, and Henry all mark the heathen premise beneath the taunt, that the more altars a people keeps the safer they are, and expose it as the exact inversion of the truth. What the Assyrian counted a stripping of Judah's defences was in fact her one true defence restored; and the envoy, reasoning from a false theology of many shrines, could not see that the God he supposed offended by the single altar was the very God who would answer for that altar's sole honour by the destruction of his host.
13:
The envoy's argument now broadens from Judah's altars to the whole record of Assyrian conquest — "know ye not what I and my fathers have done?" — and the witnesses weigh both its boast and its buried fallacy. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott observes that the Assyrian kings were fond of just such references to their predecessors, and that the Chronicler has quietly dropped the list of vanquished states given at 2 Kings 18:34, some of which had grown obscure by lapse of time. He sets the boast against the temper of the monuments, where Assurbanipal records carrying off the gods and goddesses of conquered Elam to Assyria and names nineteen of the captured deities — the very theology the envoy here presses.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch lay bare the reasoning. The description is of Sennacherib's all-conquering power, echoing 2 Kings 18:35 and Isaiah 36:20: who among all the gods of the peoples his fathers utterly destroyed was able to deliver his people out of the Assyrian's hand, that Judah's God should save her? The premise, they note, is that since the gods of nations mightier than Judah could not save them, how should Judah's lesser God prevail — a syllogism whose whole force rests on reckoning the LORD one god among many.

The reformed John Gill, treating the verse within the block he has bundled from the twelfth, and the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry both fix on that fatal confusion. Sennacherib boasted, Henry says, of his triumphs over the gods of the nations, that none of them could protect their worshippers, and thence inferred not merely how shall your God deliver you, but, as if the LORD were the feeblest of all, how much less shall your God deliver you. The witnesses do not divide. Ellicott sets the boast among its Assyrian parallels, Keil exposes its logic, Gill and Henry its blasphemy. Between them they show the envoy reasoning himself, by his own catalogue of ruined idols, straight into the impiety that would presently destroy his master's army — for the God he ranked with the gods of wood and stone was the living God who made the heavens. And the witnesses let the boast betray itself: the envoy's whole argument turns on a catalogue of conquered gods, and by parading it he unwittingly lays the ground of his master's ruin. Ellicott sets the taunt among its Assyrian parallels, Keil traces its logic step by step, Gill and Henry weigh its blasphemy; and together they show that the fatal flaw was not in the count of ruined nations but in the reckoning that made the LORD one item in that count. The gods of Hamath and Sepharvaim were indeed the work of men's hands; but the envoy, sweeping the God of Israel into the same tally, mistook the living God for a carved thing, and staked an empire on the error.
14:
The taunt is pressed to its point in a single scornful question: of all the gods of the nations his fathers had devoted to destruction, which had ever delivered its people, that the God of Hezekiah should deliver Jerusalem? The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott glosses the grim verb "utterly destroyed" as "put under the ban, devoted to destruction," the language of holy war turned to Assyrian boasting; and he refers the whole to the parallel at 2 Kings 18:35, where the same challenge is flung. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read it as the culminating form of the argument begun above: no god of any conquered land had rescued its worshippers, therefore the God of this small people can be no exception.

The reformed John Gill, still within the compass of the argument he had bundled from the twelfth verse, lets the blasphemy speak; and the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out its insolence. The envoy's how shall your God deliver you ranks the Maker of heaven and earth with the impotent idols of the nations, as though an infinite and eternal Spirit had no more power to save than they. The whole force of the sneer, Henry sees, lay in a false analogy — that because the gods of Hamath and Arpad had failed, the God of Israel must fail too — and it is precisely that false analogy which turns the boast into the blasphemy for which the Assyrian will answer.

The witnesses do not divide, and they let the very structure of the verse convict its speaker. Ellicott fixes the ban-language and the parallel; Keil the pitiless logic; Gill and Henry the affront to the living God. Between them they show the envoy building his case with perfect confidence upon a single unexamined assumption — that Jehovah is a god like the rest — and so preparing, all unwitting, the ground of his own overthrow; for the question which of the gods could deliver was about to receive an answer he had not reckoned on, in the destruction of his master's host by the God he had dared to number with the dead idols of the earth. And the witnesses let the sneer measure the distance between the envoy's confidence and his doom: never was a man so sure of a conclusion built on a premise so false. Ellicott, Keil, Gill, and Henry all fasten on that premise — that Jehovah is a god like the rest — and show it the hinge on which the whole boast swung and the whole army fell. The question was fair as rhetoric, for no god of the nations had delivered its people; but it reckoned without the one God who is no idol, and it is the answer to that very question, given in the smitten camp, that the Chronicler is hastening the reader toward.
15:
The speech reaches its climax in a direct summons to distrust: let not Hezekiah deceive you, believe him not. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the closing challenge in its full arrogance — "much less will your gods deliver you," or "much more will your gods not deliver you" — and compares the parallel taunt at Isaiah 37:10-11. He lays bare the pagan theology beneath it: by the ancient reckoning, the gods of strong nations were strong gods, and since Assyria had beaten nations stronger than Judah, her armies ignorantly supposed they had beaten stronger deities than the God of Judah. He notes that some Hebrew manuscripts and all the versions give the verb in the singular, "much less will your god deliver you," narrowing the scorn to the one God of Israel.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch mark the verse as the summing-up of the whole harangue: no god of any nation or kingdom had delivered his people out of the Assyrian's hand, nor out of his fathers', how much less should Judah's? The reformed John Gill, closing the bundle of verses he had taken together, lets the false inference stand exposed by its own repetition.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the force of the peroration. Sennacherib had reasoned himself, from god to god of the ruined nations, into placing the LORD not merely among them but beneath them all — how much less shall your God deliver you — as if he were less able to help than any of the idols. And it was here, Henry notes, that the envoys, learning insolence from their master, spoke and would presently write more than even he had bidden them against the God of Israel. The witnesses do not divide. Ellicott exposes the heathen premise and the textual variant, Keil the logic of the summons, Gill the repeated fallacy, Henry the crowning blasphemy. Between them they show the Assyrian daring the people to disbelieve their king by disbelieving their God — and staking the whole issue of the war on the one proposition heaven was about to disprove. And the witnesses let the peroration seal the envoy's guilt: he had begun by questioning the people's trust in their king and ends by daring them to distrust their God, so that the whole speech is one long argument for unbelief. Ellicott exposes the pagan reckoning of strong nations and strong gods, Keil the remorseless logic, Gill the wearisome repetition of the lie, Henry the crowning insolence; and all agree that the summons reached its farthest point here, where the Assyrian staked the outcome of the war on the single proposition that the God of Israel could not save. It was the boldest word he ever spoke, and the last before heaven answered it.
16:
The narrator pauses to record that the envoys did not stop at the reported speech: his servants spake yet more. The reformed John Gill takes the note as an open confession that the account is not exhaustive — they said more than what is here set down, as may be read in the fuller records of Kings and Isaiah. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott agrees that the verse shows the Chronicler does not profess to give a full report, and renders the object of the railing sharply: they spoke against Jehovah the true God, the very charge Isaiah's answer would fling back — whom hast thou reproached and blasphemed? the Holy One of Israel — at Isaiah 37:23.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch let the sentence stand within the flow of the deliverance narrative, a bridge from the reported taunts to the letters and the outcry that follow; the servants' speech against the LORD and against his servant Hezekiah is the swelling of the blasphemy that will draw down the judgment.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry finds in the verse a solemn observation. In the instructions Sennacherib gave, he says, the king said more than enough; but as if his blasphemies had been too little, his servants, who had learned insolence from their master, spoke yet more than he bade them, against the Lord God and against his servant Hezekiah. And Henry marks the pairing of the two names as no accident: God resents what is said against his servants, and will reckon for it, as surely as for what is said against himself. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Ellicott fix the incompleteness of the record and the object of the railing; Keil sets it in the movement toward deliverance; Henry draws the lesson that the LORD makes common cause with his reproached servant. Between them they show the blasphemy overflowing its bounds — masters and servants alike heaping words upon the God of Israel and upon the king who trusted him — and they leave the reader in no doubt that every such word was being written down in a book that heaven would open at the reckoning. And the witnesses let the overflow of the blasphemy foreshadow its judgment: the servants, not content with their master's script, added railings of their own, so that the sin swelled past its bounds and hastened its reckoning. Gill marks the record's own confession of incompleteness, Ellicott the object of the railing named as the true God, Keil its place in the march toward deliverance, Henry the solidarity of the LORD with the servant reproached in the same breath as himself. Together they leave the impression the verse means to leave: that a blasphemy multiplied is a blasphemy ripening, and that the God who kept silence through it all was not indifferent but only biding the night of his answer.
17:
Beyond the spoken taunts came written ones, and the witnesses attend to the letters and to their place in the story. The reformed John Gill and the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke both refer the reader to the fuller record, where Sennacherib's letters are told at 2 Kings 19:9 and following. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the clause "and letters wrote he to reproach," echoing Isaiah 37:23, and untangles the chronology. Sennacherib wrote demanding submission only after the failure of the mission of the Tartan and his companions at 2 Kings 19:8-14; so that, had the Chronicler been careful of strict sequence, this verse would have followed rather than preceded the two that come after it. As it is, the notice of the letters is thrown in here as a parenthesis, in the midst of the account of the envoys' behaviour — one more instance, Ellicott observes, of the abbreviation the writer studies throughout.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch let the letters carry forward the single argument of the whole assault: as the gods of the nations of other lands had not delivered their people out of the Assyrian's hand, so, the writing declared, neither should the God of Hezekiah deliver his.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry finds the written blasphemy the graver for being deliberate. To rail in speech is bad enough; but Sennacherib railed in writing, Henry notes, which, being more considered, is so much the worse — setting down in a letter, as with a cool pen, that the Lord God of Israel was a cipher and an empty name like all the rest. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Clarke send us to the fuller history; Ellicott fixes the wording and rescues the order of events; Keil marks the continuity of the taunt; Henry weighs the peculiar guilt of a blasphemy composed and written. Between them they show the enemy committing his impiety to paper, so that the very letters that were meant to break Jerusalem's faith became, when Hezekiah spread them before the LORD, the indictment on which the God of Israel would act. And the witnesses let the written word weigh heavier than the spoken: a taunt shouted in the heat of a parley may be the folly of a moment, but a letter is composed, considered, and sealed, and Sennacherib's letter carried his impiety in a form that could be spread out and read. Gill and Clarke send us to the fuller record, Ellicott rescues the true order of events, Keil the single thread of the taunt, Henry the deliberate malice of ink; and they leave the reader with the irony the story turns upon — that a document meant to terrify Jerusalem into surrender became, once carried into the temple, the written charge on which the Assyrian was judged.
18:
The envoys raise their voices to the watchmen on the wall, and the witnesses note both the tongue they used and the end they sought. The reformed John Gill identifies the criers as Sennacherib's messengers, Rabshakeh chief among them, who cried in the Jews' own speech to the people of Jerusalem upon the wall, though they had been asked to speak rather in the Syrian tongue. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott observes that the Septuagint and Vulgate read the singular, "he cried" — that is, the Rabshakeh — and refers to the fuller scene at 2 Kings 18:26-28. The purpose he takes to be the Chronicler's own summary of the speech reported there: to affright the people, and to terrify and scare them, that the city might be taken. The verb "to affright," he adds, is a rare one, met besides only in Nehemiah 6:9 and once in Samuel.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch let the loud outcry in the Jews' language stand as the deliberate stroke it was — a bid to reach past the king's ambassadors to the common people on the wall, and by sheer terror to loosen their resolve before ever a siege-engine was raised.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads that design as the heart of the whole assault. All this shouting, he says, was intended to frighten the people from their hope in God, as David's enemies sought to fright him with there is no help for him in God at Psalms 71:11; the Assyrian hoped to take the city by weakening the hands of those who should defend it. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the criers and the tongue, Ellicott the singular speaker and the aim of terror, Keil the reaching past the king to the people, Henry the war upon their faith. Between them they show that the whole loud performance beneath the wall was aimed not at the stones but at the spirits of the defenders — an attempt to conquer Jerusalem by panic, which the steady word of a believing king had already forearmed his people to withstand. And the witnesses let the shout beneath the wall reveal the whole aim of the siege: not yet to breach the stones but to break the spirits, reaching over the heads of the king's ambassadors to the watchmen in their own tongue, that terror might do the work no engine had yet done. Gill fixes the criers and their chosen speech, Ellicott the single loud voice and its purpose of scaring, Keil the reaching past the throne to the people, Henry the assault upon their hope in God. Together they show a strategy as old as the tempter himself — to conquer by fear what could not be conquered by force — and a people whose king had already, by his steady word at the gate, taught them to stand.
19:
The narrator fixes the exact sin that will bring the Assyrian down: the envoys spoke against the God of Jerusalem as though he were one of the idols of the nations. The reformed John Gill marks the enormity by naming the God they reviled — the only living and true God, whom the inhabitants of Jerusalem professed and worshipped in the temple there — set by the blasphemers on a level with the dead gods of the heathen. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes that the Chronicler, instead of repeating the envoys' offers to the people, deliberately dwells on this one blasphemy against the God of Israel, because it was the very cause of the Assyrian overthrow. "The work of the hands of man," he adds, is a reminiscence of Hezekiah's own prayer at 2 Kings 19:18, where the king pleads that the gods the Assyrians had burned were no gods, but the work of human hands, wood and stone.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry seizes on the title "the God of Jerusalem," which, he says, he is here called because that was the place he had chosen to put his name. This proud blasphemer compared the great Jehovah, the Maker of heaven and earth, with the dunghill gods of the nations, the work of men's hands, and thought him no more able to deliver his worshippers than they were to deliver theirs — as if an infinite and eternal Spirit had no more wisdom and power than a stone, or the stock of a tree.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill names the living God dishonoured, Ellicott marks why the Chronicler singles out this blasphemy and traces its language to Hezekiah's prayer, Henry weighs the folly of levelling the Creator with carved wood and stone. Between them they show the pivot of the whole narrative: the envoys' every earlier taunt had been political, an assault on the people's nerve, but here they cross into sacrilege, and it is precisely this — the naming of the God of Jerusalem among the idols — that turns the quarrel from a siege into a contest between the Assyrian and the Almighty, which the next verses will decide. And the witnesses let the verse mark the exact moment the Assyrian sealed his fate: while his taunts had been political, aimed at the nerve of the defenders, he might have withdrawn and lived; but here he crosses into sacrilege, and the crossing is fatal. Gill names the living God dishonoured, Ellicott shows why the Chronicler dwells on this blasphemy above all the offers he passes over, Henry the madness of matching the Maker with a carved stock; and together they mark this as the pivot on which the whole story turns, from a contest of armies to a contest between a boaster and the Almighty — a contest whose issue was never for a moment in doubt.
20:
Against the blasphemy the king and the prophet answer not with a sortie but with a cry to heaven, and the witnesses dwell on the partnership in prayer. The reformed John Gill observes that though the record before us tells only of Hezekiah's prayer, Isaiah beyond doubt prayed also, since the king had asked it and the prophet received in return a message from the LORD to send him. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the opening "upon this" — that is, upon the Assyrian blasphemies, which Hezekiah urged in his prayer at 2 Kings 19:16 and to which Isaiah's answer replied at Isaiah 37:23. The parallels, he notes, do not say that Isaiah prayed, but they record that the king sent a deputation of his nobles to the prophet to beg his prayers for the remnant that were left at 2 Kings 19:2-4; and "cried to heaven" he compares with the like phrase at 2 Chronicles 30:27.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry finds here the duty and the interest of the church's friends: in the day of distress, to pray and cry to heaven. It was a happy time, he says, when the king and the prophet thus joined in prayer; and he draws the counsel wide — is any troubled, is any terrified? let him pray. Praying is called crying to heaven, Henry notes, because in prayer we are to eye God as our Father in heaven, whence he beholds the children of men and where he has prepared his throne.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill supplies the prophet's unrecorded prayer, Ellicott the occasion in the blasphemy and the deputation that sought Isaiah's intercession, Henry the blessedness of king and prophet crying together. Between them they show the true weapon of the beleaguered city: over against an enemy who has railed at the God of Jerusalem, the king who had strengthened his walls now turns from the walls to heaven, and the prophet with him — so that the answer to the Assyrian's letters is a prayer, and the answer to the prayer, as the next verse tells, will be an angel. And the witnesses let the prayer stand as the true turning of the siege: the king who had walled and watered his city now lays down every weapon but this, and the prophet kneels with him. Gill recovers Isaiah's unrecorded prayer from the message he received in return, Ellicott the blasphemy that occasioned the cry and the nobles sent to beg the prophet's intercession, Henry the blessedness of a throne and a pulpit joined in supplication. Together they show that Jerusalem's defence was, in the end, neither in her stones nor in her stratagems but in her God, sought by a king and a prophet crying together to heaven — and that the loudest boast of earth is answered soonest when it is answered from above.
21:
The answer to that prayer is the great catastrophe of the chapter — an angel sent, an army destroyed, an emperor slain in his own temple — and the witnesses marvel, explain, and gently differ over the means. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note that the number of the slain is not given here, as it was not the point; the point is that the whole Assyrian host was annihilated, so that Sennacherib returned in disgrace to his land, where his own sons cut him down in the house of his god. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott supplies from the parallel at 2 Kings 19:35 the number the Chronicler omits, a hundred and eighty-five thousand; renders the verb "he hid," that is, caused to disappear; and identifies the parricides, whom the Chronicler leaves nameless after his manner with foreign names, as Adrammelech and Sharezer, who escaped into Ararat. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke names them too, and the god Nisroch in whose house the murder was done.

Over the instrument of the slaughter the witnesses divide without quarrelling. The reformed John Gill sets out the options: the Targum says the Word of the LORD sent Gabriel; Josephus took the angel to be the pestilence; others suppose a hot pestilential wind, the poison of the eastern deserts, which destroys multitudes at a stroke — but, Gill insists, be it what it may, it was sent of God and did its execution by his power according to his word. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley and the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry follow the Targum, that the Word of the LORD sent Gabriel, and that the work was done with lightning, in the passover night — the very night in which the firstborn of Egypt were slain. Ellicott records yet another view, that of Hitzig, who spoke of a great natural miracle and thought Isaiah composed Psalms 46-48 to commemorate it.

Henry lingers on the twofold stroke of justice. The army was cut off by the sword of an angel, which triumphed particularly over the mighty men of valour, the leaders and captains who had defied the sword of any man — for God delights to abase the proud and secure. And the king, having been thus disgraced, was cut off by the sword of his own sons: mortified first and then murdered, shamed and then slain. The witnesses do not divide on the substance — an angelic judgment, wholly of God — though they weigh its means variously, some naming Gabriel and the fire of passover night, others a plague or a pestilential wind. What all confess is that the God whom the Assyrian had ranked with idols answered the blasphemy in a single night, and left the boaster to die by the hands that came forth of his own bowels.
22:
The historian sums up the deliverance in his own voice, and the witnesses attend to both the theology and a knot in the text. The reformed John Gill reads the summary plainly: thus the LORD saved Hezekiah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, as most clearly appeared, for no stroke had been struck but by him. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott marks the whole verse as the Chronicler's own comment on the story, comparing the like notice at 2 Kings 18:7, and observes that some manuscripts fittingly add "his enemies" to "the hand of all," a word that may have dropped from the text.

Over the closing phrase a genuine difference opens. The received Hebrew ends "and guided them on every side," which Ellicott calls unusual and would emend, with the Septuagint and Vulgate, to "and gave them rest round about" — a phrase, he notes, thoroughly at home with the Chronicler, as at 2 Chronicles 15:15 and 2 Chronicles 20:30. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch defend the text as it stands: the verb means to lead with the added sense of care and protection, as in Psalms 31:3 and Isaiah 49:10, and here, he protected them round about. Though the phrase Bertheau prefers is indeed common with the Chronicler, Keil judges it improbable that the received reading arose from it by a copyist's error, and so keeps the harder word.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, reading the common version, finds a whole providence in it. The LORD saved Jerusalem, he says, not only from the hand of Sennacherib but from the hand of all others; such a deliverance was an earnest of much mercy in store. And he guided them means he guarded them on every side; for God defends his people by directing them, showing them what they should do, and so saving them from what is designed against them. The witnesses do not divide on the mercy, only on the word that names it. Gill and Henry rest on the received text and its guarding grace; Ellicott would read "gave them rest"; Keil holds the harder "protected them round about." Between them they leave the verse where the Chronicler set it — a plain confession that the whole rescue, by wall and water and angel alike, was in the end the LORD's own doing. And the witnesses let the summary gather the whole chapter into one confession: wall, water, and angel alike were but the instruments of a single Deliverer, so that the credit of the rescue returns wholly to the LORD. Gill, Ellicott, Keil, and Henry differ only over the word that names the mercy — whether God led, protected, or gave rest — but not over its author; and they leave the verse as a doxology in the historian's own voice, that the God who was reproached among the idols has saved his people from the hand of all their enemies.
23:
The deliverance bears fruit in tribute and homage, and the witnesses weigh who came bearing gifts and why. The reformed John Gill takes the "many" to include neighbouring nations, who, convinced that so wonderful a deliverance had been wrought by the LORD God of Israel and by him only, devoted their offerings to his service in the temple. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch agree that the word is not to be confined to Israelites but denotes chiefly the surrounding peoples, who by the destruction of the Assyrian army were themselves freed from a dreaded enemy, and so felt moved to show their reverence for the God of Israel.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds that the offering is the minchah, a gift or tribute, and that the presents brought to Hezekiah came from such as the envoys of Merodach-baladan of Babylon, named at 2 Kings 20:12, and probably from neighbouring peoples like the Philistines, relieved of the Assyrian pressure; he was magnified, he renders literally, lifted up, to the eyes of all the nations. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the double homage with a shrewd eye: men plainly saw that Jehovah was the protector of the land, and they saw too that God was Hezekiah's friend and would undertake for him, and they did not wish to have such a man for an enemy.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the meaning. Strangers were induced by the great work to supplicate God's favour, and enemies to deprecate his wrath, and both brought their gifts to his temple; while many brought presents to Hezekiah himself, in token of the honour they now paid him. By the favour of God, Henry concludes, enemies are lost and friends gained. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Keil fix the nations that came, Ellicott the Babylonian and Philistine bearers and the king's exaltation, Clarke the mixed motive of reverence and self-interest, Henry the double tide of homage to God and to his servant. Between them they show the reward of the deliverance overflowing the walls of Jerusalem: a God vindicated before the watching nations, and a king lifted in their eyes because the LORD had lifted him — the very magnifying, the witnesses will soon note, against which his own heart would need to be guarded. And the witnesses let the tribute measure the completeness of the deliverance: the God who had been reviled among the idols is now honoured with gifts from the very nations that had trembled at Assyria, and the king who had been mocked is now courted by them. Gill and Keil fix the reverence of the neighbouring peoples, Ellicott the Babylonian and Philistine bearers, Clarke the mingled awe and self-interest, Henry the double homage to God and his servant. Together they show the vindication overflowing Judah's borders — yet they set beside it the quiet warning that a king so magnified in the eyes of all the nations would find that very honour the hardest of his trials.
24:
The narrative turns from the nation's rescue to the king's own sickbed, and the witnesses observe how much the Chronicler compresses. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott remarks that this single verse epitomises the whole long account of 2 Kings 20:1-11 and Isaiah 38: Hezekiah was sick unto dying, and prayed, and God spake unto him by the mouth of Isaiah and gave him a sign — the recession of the shadow upon the dial of Ahaz, the emphatic word set first in the Hebrew, "and a sign he gave him." The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch agree that the Chronicle offers only hints of the matter, and note that the two verbs, he spake and he gave, have the same subject, God, who answered the prayer through his prophet and confirmed the answer by a miracle.

The reformed John Gill and the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke both simply send the reader to the fuller narrative in Kings for the sickness, the prayer, and the sign. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, beginning the last section of Hezekiah's story, gathers it under three heads — his sickness and recovery, his sin and repentance, and the honour done him living and dead — and reads this verse as the first: the disease seemed likely to be mortal, but in the extremity of it he prayed, and God answered him and gave him a sign that he should recover, the going back of the sun ten degrees.

The witnesses do not divide. Ellicott and Keil fix the compression and the sign; Gill and Clarke defer to the parallel; Henry frames the whole close of the reign. Between them they show the Chronicler content to touch lightly what Kings and Isaiah had told at length, keeping his eye on his own purpose — for what he most wishes to record is not the miracle of the shadow but the peril that followed the mercy, when a king raised from the gates of death would find recovery a harder trial of his heart than sickness had been. The sign that turned back the sun is set down almost in passing, that the reader may hurry on to the pride it occasioned and the humbling that healed it. And the witnesses let the brevity itself instruct: where Kings and Isaiah spread the sickness, the prayer, and the sign over many verses, the Chronicler compresses all into a line, because his interest lies not in the wonder but in its sequel. Ellicott and Keil mark the sign as the shadow drawn back on the dial, God answering through the prophet; Gill and Clarke defer to the fuller record; Henry frames the three heads under which the whole close of the reign will be told. Together they show a historian who tells the miracle almost in passing, that he may dwell on the graver matter it occasioned — the pride of a heart lifted up by mercy, and the humbling that alone could heal it.
25:
The mercy is followed by ingratitude, and the witnesses probe the sin of a lifted-up heart. The reformed John Gill reads "the benefit" broadly, of both deliverances — the rescue from Assyria and the recovery from sickness — for which Hezekiah rendered no fit return. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch locate the pride precisely: in his sickness he had promised to walk in humility all his days, as Isaiah 38:15 records, yet after his recovery his heart grew proud, and the pride showed itself above all in his displaying his treasures to the Babylonian embassy in idle trust, told at 2 Kings 20:12-15. Therefore wrath came upon him and upon Judah and Jerusalem, who shared the king's temper; and Isaiah proclaimed that wrath in the prophecy that all his treasures should be carried to Babylon and some of his sons made courtiers there, at 2 Kings 20:16-18.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses fill in the psychology. Adam Clarke says the king got into a vain confidence, took pleasure in his riches, and vainly showed them off; John Wesley traces the swelling to three causes at once — the prodigious victory over the Assyrians, the miraculous recovery from sickness, and the honour of an embassy from the great king of Babylon — all of which raised in him too high an opinion of himself, as if these things had been done for his own piety and virtue. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds that Judah and Jerusalem shared the guilty pride and the confidence in an arm of flesh.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry drives the lesson home. Hezekiah was proud of the honour God had put upon him and the honour his neighbours paid him, and it exalted him above measure; when he had destroyed other idolatries, Henry observes sharply, he began to idolize himself. The aggravation was that he made even God's favours the food and fuel of his pride, rendering not again according to the benefit done him; and though it was but a heart-sin, and the outward act — showing his treasures to a friend — seemed innocent, yet wrath came upon him and his kingdom, for pride is a sin God hates as much as any, and particularly in his own people. The witnesses do not divide. Gill names the unrequited mercy, Keil and Ellicott the broken vow and the coming judgment, Clarke and Wesley the sources of the swelling, Henry the self-idolatry beneath it. Between them they show how near mercy and danger lie — a man delivered from death and from an empire, undone in his heart by the very deliverances that should have humbled him.
26:
Pride is met by penitence, and the witnesses trace the humbling that turned the wrath aside. The reformed John Gill confesses that the manner of the humiliation is not told, but supposes it took the usual forms — sackcloth, fasting, prayer, and the confession of sin. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott finds the humbling in Hezekiah's very answer to Isaiah's sentence: when the prophet foretold the carrying away of his treasures and his sons, the king humbly acquiesced in the will of Jehovah — good is the word of the LORD which thou hast spoken, and there shall be peace and truth in my days, at 2 Kings 20:19. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch draw out the consequence: because he humbled himself, the threatened judgment was postponed, and broke over the royal house and the whole kingdom only later, in the Chaldean invasion.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the repentance as a waking from sleep — Hezekiah grew sorry for his sin and deprecated the wrath, and the divine displeasure was turned away. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the verse into a cluster of rules. Though God may suffer his people to fall into sin, he will not suffer them to lie still in it; heart-sins are to be repented of, though they go no further; self-humiliation is a necessary branch of repentance; and pride of heart in particular is a sin for which we ought especially to humble ourselves. Henry marks too that the people humbled themselves with their king, either knowing they had shared his sin or fearing to share his punishment — as when David's pride in numbering Israel brought a plague on all.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill supposes the outward acts of penitence, Ellicott finds it in the king's meek acceptance of the sentence, Keil marks the reprieve it won, Clarke the turning away of wrath, Henry the lessons of a repented heart-sin. Between them they show the true recovery of Hezekiah — not the healing of his body, but the humbling of his spirit — and the mercy that follows it: that because the king and his people bowed, the storm foretold did not fall in their day, and the reign closed in the peace that repentance had bought. And the witnesses let that peace be the last word on the sin: the God who had been provoked by pride was appeased by penitence, and the storm foretold was held back from Hezekiah's day — a mercy Gill, Ellicott, Keil, Clarke, and Henry all trace to the single fact that the king, and his people with him, humbled themselves. It is the pattern the Chronicler loves to show, that judgment threatened is judgment deferred wherever a heart is truly bowed, and that the truest strength of a reign lies not in its treasures but in its readiness to repent.
27:
The record turns to the king's wealth, and the witnesses set his treasuries in the line of Israel's great and prosperous kings. The reformed John Gill traces the riches to their recent sources — the spoil of the Assyrian camp and the presents sent him afterward by the nations. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch place Hezekiah beside Jehoshaphat, Solomon, and David, each of whom attained to riches and glory; he made himself treasure-chambers for silver, gold, precious stones, spices, shields, and all manner of splendid furniture, the shields named to stand for weapons in general, and the whole collection recalling the house of his precious things that he would show the Babylonians at 2 Kings 20:13.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms the pattern, comparing the like notices of David at 1 Chronicles 29:28 and Solomon at 2 Chronicles 1:12; he takes the shields, like Solomon's golden and Rehoboam's brazen ones, to suggest arms in general, and renders "all manner of pleasant jewels" literally "all vessels of desire," costly implements and utensils of every sort. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke glosses the same phrase, keley chemdah, as desirable vessels or utensils.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the whole inventory as the honour God's providence did Hezekiah while he lived: he had exceeding much riches and honour, replenished his stores, victualled his forts, fortified his city, and did all that he wished to do, for God had given him very much substance. The witnesses do not divide. Gill names the sources of the wealth, Keil and Ellicott set it among the treasures of the greatest kings and mark the shields and the vessels of desire, Clarke the precious utensils, Henry the providence behind the plenty. Between them they show a king restored, enriched, and honoured — and the reader who has just heard of his pride cannot but feel the quiet warning in the catalogue, that these very treasures, the gift of God, were the same he would one day display in the vanity that drew down the word of judgment. The wealth is real and God-given; the danger is that a lifted-up heart should make it, as it once made it, the fuel of its pride. And the witnesses let the inventory carry its double sense: it is at once the record of a blessing and the seedbed of a temptation, for the treasures God gave were the very treasures pride would misuse. Gill traces their source in the Assyrian spoil and the nations' gifts, Keil and Ellicott range them among the riches of David and Solomon, Clarke glosses the vessels of desire, Henry reads the whole as the honour providence did the king; and together they show that wealth in a good man's hand is a gift to be held with trembling.
28:
The catalogue of plenty runs on from treasure to harvest and herd, and the witnesses attend to the storehouses and stalls of a well-ordered realm. The reformed John Gill takes the increase of corn and wine and oil for the produce of the king's own fields, vineyards, and oliveyards, set under officers as David's had been. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch describe the several provisions: magazines for the agricultural produce, and stalls for all manner of cattle and for the herds, exactly as David had appointed at 1 Chronicles 27:25 and Uzziah at 2 Chronicles 26:10. They note the philological curiosities: the word for storehouses is a transposition of a root meaning to heap up, the phrase for cattle is a Hebrew way of saying all kinds of cattle, and the term for stalls, occurring here only, is a transposed form of the more usual word.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds his own notes on the vocabulary. Storehouses are magazines such as those built in Egypt at Exodus 1:11; "all manner of beasts" means every kind of cattle; and the closing clause, which the common version gives as "cotes for flocks," reads in the Hebrew "and flocks for folds," the words having been transposed, he judges, by some copyist — a reading the Septuagint and Vulgate confirm with their "folds for the flocks."

The witnesses do not divide; they simply share the labour of description. Gill fixes the produce and its overseers, Keil the range of the stores and stalls with their curious spellings, Ellicott the sense of the magazines and the transposed clause. Between them they turn a dry inventory into the picture of a kingdom made abundant and secure — grain and wine and oil laid up against scarcity, cattle and flocks housed and multiplied — and they let it stand as one more evidence of the substance God had given the king, the outward token of a reign that, whatever the peril of its wealth, was in its ordering the very image of prosperity blessed from above. And the witnesses let the humble details do their quiet work: the storehouses and stalls, the transposed Hebrew words that Keil and Ellicott turn over, are no mere antiquarian trivia but the visible tokens of a realm ordered and secure under God's blessing. Gill sets the produce under its overseers as in David's day, Keil ranks the provision with that of David and Uzziah, Ellicott mends the copyist's transposed clause. Together they show a kingdom in which grain and wine and oil, cattle and flocks, are gathered and multiplied — not for luxury's sake but as the sober husbandry of a king who knew that plenty, like safety, is God's gift and must be well kept; and the very fullness of the record becomes a testimony to the substance heaven had bestowed.
29:
The account of the king's substance closes with a word over which the witnesses genuinely differ — did Hezekiah provide himself cities, or something else? The reformed John Gill keeps the plain sense: cities in which he had his storehouses and stalls, with convenient dwellings for those who tended his cattle great and small; he notes that some copies of the Vulgate even read six cities. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads it likewise of towns, which the king repaired, fortified, and beautified for the honour and safety of his kingdom.

The grammatical-historical witnesses demur. Keil and Delitzsch argue that the word cannot here denote ordinary cities; it must mean either watch-towers, from a root signifying to watch, or dwelling-places for herds and cattle, since the Hebrew term is used at 2 Kings 17:9 of any enclosed place, from a watch-tower to a fenced city. Charles Ellicott renders it outright "watch-towers," forts for the protection of the flocks and herds, comparing the besieged city of Isaiah 1:8 and the towers Uzziah built in the desert at 2 Chronicles 26:10. So the debate stands: whether the verse tells of fortified towns for the realm's safety, or of towers and folds for the safety of the king's vast cattle.

On the ground of the whole notice the witnesses are one. God had given him substance very much — wealth in kind, Ellicott explains, especially cattle, the very sense the word bears at 2 Chronicles 31:3; and the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the clause as the spring of all the rest, that the king could provide so richly because God had given him so much. Gill and Wesley keep the cities, Keil and Ellicott prefer the watch-towers, but none doubts the point the verse exists to make: that Hezekiah's flocks and stores and strongholds alike were the overflow of a substance not of his own getting but of God's giving, so that even the record of his riches is turned, in the witnesses' hands, into an acknowledgment of the hand that bestowed them. And the witnesses let the small debate serve the larger confession: whether Hezekiah built cities or watch-towers, whether he housed his people or his herds, the verse ends by tracing all of it to a single source — God had given him substance very much. Gill and Wesley keep the towns, Keil and Ellicott the towers and folds, but the disagreement is over the masonry, not the meaning; for all four read the closing clause as the ground of the whole, that the king's abundance was not the fruit of his own getting. Between the reformed and grammatical-historical readings there is thus no quarrel about the point the Chronicler most wishes to make: that even a catalogue of possessions is, rightly read, a hymn to the Giver.
30:
Among the king's works the Chronicler singles out the great waterwork, and the witnesses trace the course of the Gihon he mastered. The reformed John Gill, citing the traveller Maundrell, describes the pool of Gihon as a stately basin without the Bethlehem gate to the west, and reports the old identification, from Procopius, of Gihon with Siloam; the upper watercourse was one of its two streams. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch explain the engineering: Hezekiah covered the upper outlet of the waters of Gihon and brought them down westward by a subterranean channel into the city of David — the same work begun in the emergency of v.3 — and they note that he prospered in all his works, the refrain of 2 Chronicles 31:21.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses fill in the detail. Adam Clarke says he made canals to bring the waters from the west side to the city of David; John Wesley describes the rivulet's two streams, the upper gathered into the upper pool of Isaiah 7:3 and the lower into the lower pool of Isaiah 22:9, and reckons the diverting of the former into the city by pipes a work of great art and labour. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms it from the parallel at 2 Kings 20:20, where the same great work is named in the summing-up of Hezekiah's reign — he made the pool, and the conduit, and brought the water into the city — adding that the Chronicler here gives the further details.
