The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry ties the work back to its origin in the war: the turning of the watercourse of Gihon was done upon occasion of Sennacherib's invasion, when the springs were stopped at v.4; the water that had run into the old and upper pools he gathered into a new place, for the greater convenience of the city; and he prospered in all his works, for they were good works. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Wesley trace the pools and streams, Keil and Ellicott and Clarke the underground conduit into the city of David, Henry the wartime occasion and the prosperity that crowned it. Between them they show a monument of the king's wisdom that outlasted the siege — a hidden channel bringing living water within the wall — and a standing sign that the same God who sent the angel had prospered the spade.
31:
The chapter's last event is the embassy from Babylon and the trial it became, and the witnesses probe both the errand of the envoys and the strange providence that left the king to himself. Over the errand a real difference appears. The reformed John Gill holds that they came to inquire of the miracle of the sun's going back ten degrees, the Chaldeans being much given to astrology — and he sets aside two other views, the Targum's that they came to see the two tables of stone in the ark, and Grotius's that they came to ask about the destruction of the Assyrian army. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads it the same way: the wonder is the sign of v.24, and such an inquiry is wholly in keeping with what the monuments show of Babylon, the home of divination and augury, where the retrograde shadow would fascinate the astronomers of the temple-towers. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley allow it might have been either the going back of the sun or the fall of the Assyrians — the sun being the Babylonians' god, and the Assyrians their rivals — that drew the curious embassy.

On the providence the witnesses converge. Keil and Delitzsch fix the sense of the connecting word: it is not "howbeit" but "and accordingly," for God permitted Hezekiah to be lifted up on this occasion and to commit the iniquity that brought misfortune, not to plunge him into ruin but to try and to humble him. Ellicott explains that "to try" is the same word as "to tempt," as at Psalms 95:9, and that "that he might know all in his heart" means to bring out and make manifest what was latent there; the Searcher of hearts knew the issue beforehand, and speaks after the manner of men, as a chemist proves an unknown substance to learn its nature.

The wesleyan-arminian and puritan-evangelical voices draw the lesson. Wesley says God left him to himself and suffered Satan to try him, that he might know he had infirmities and sins as well as virtues. Henry puts it most memorably: God, who could by his grace have prevented the sin, permitted it for holy ends, that by the trial and his weakness in it, it might be known what was in his heart — God left him to himself to be proud of his wealth, to keep him from being proud of his holiness. The witnesses do not, in the end, divide. Gill, Ellicott, Henry, and Wesley weigh what the Babylonians sought — the astronomical wonder most of all, though some allow the Assyrian overthrow, and the Targum the tables in the ark; and all agree on what God sought — not Hezekiah's fall, but the showing of his heart to himself, that a man raised so high might learn how much he still needed grace.
32:
The reign draws toward its close with the customary reference to the sources, and the witnesses attend to the naming of Isaiah's book. The reformed John Gill glosses "his goodness" as the king's acts of piety and liberality. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the word as pious deeds, the same term used at 2 Chronicles 6:42, and identify the vision of Isaiah as the book of that prophet's prophecies. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke likewise points the reader to Isaiah himself, in the chapters that tell Hezekiah's story at Isaiah 36-39.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott brings a textual nicety. Comparing the parallel at 2 Kings 20:20, he would omit the "and" before "in the book of the kings," so that the vision of Isaiah is named not as a separate work but as a section of that larger book of the kings of Judah and Israel — where the older history had said simply the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah. It is one more trace of the Chronicler's own sources and his manner of citing them.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the notice for its honour. That the prophet Isaiah wrote the life and reign of Hezekiah, his acts and his goodness, is itself part of the king's honour, Henry says, that his piety should be recorded and remembered for an example to others. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Keil fix the pious deeds and the prophet's book, Clarke sends us to Isaiah's own chapters, Ellicott mends the citation, Henry weighs the honour of a life worth the writing. Between them they show the Chronicler closing his account as he has kept it throughout — with his eye on the goodness of the king rather than the mere annals of his wars, and with the memory of a godly reign entrusted, fittingly, to the pen of the very prophet who had stood beside him through the invasion, the sickness, and the fall. And the witnesses let the source-notice bear its own testimony: that the record of Hezekiah's reign rests on the vision of Isaiah shows, Ellicott and Keil agree, a real authority behind the Chronicle beyond the canonical Kings, while the naming of the prophet honours both the writer and the king he wrote of. Gill reads the goodness as piety and liberality, Keil as pious deeds, Clarke points to Isaiah's own chapters, Ellicott mends the citation, Henry weighs the honour of a life worth recording. Together they show the Chronicler faithful to his manner to the last — passing lightly over the wars and dwelling on the goodness, so that Hezekiah's true monument is not a tomb or a treasury but the written record of his faith.
33:
The king is laid to rest with unusual honour, and the witnesses weigh both the place of his grave and the tribute of his people. The reformed John Gill notes only that he slept with his fathers, the settled idiom for death, and the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the burial in the chiefest of the sepulchres as the respect paid to one who, since David, had been the best of all their kings.

Over that phrase the grammatical-historical witnesses offer a soberer reading. Charles Ellicott would render it not "the chiefest" but "the ascent" — the way up to the royal tombs — and infers, since Hezekiah's successors Manasseh, Amon, and Josiah were likewise not laid in the tombs of the kings, that the old royal sepulchres were by now full. Keil and Delitzsch reason the same way: he was buried on the height of the graves of the sons of David, perhaps because there was no longer room in the hereditary burying-place, so that special graves had to be prepared on higher ground. So a genuine difference stands over the words: whether they mark the highest honour, a place among the chief of the kings, or simply a new plot above the crowded tombs of David's line.

On the honour itself the witnesses agree. They did him honour at his death, a phrase, Ellicott notes, found here only, both he and Keil taking it of a great burning of spices such as was made for Asa at 2 Chronicles 16:14. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the whole verse as the honour done a good king by the consciences of men: they made as great a burning for him as for Asa, and lamented him as they would afterward lament Josiah; and though the generality of the people had not heartily complied with his reforming, yet they could not but praise his endeavours, and his memory was blessed among them. It is a debt, Henry adds, that we owe to those who have been eminently useful in their day, to do them honour at their death. The witnesses do not divide on the reverence, only on the reading of the chiefest. Gill, Clarke, and Henry hear in it the highest honour; Ellicott and Keil, a grave above the full sepulchres of David's sons. Between them they lay Hezekiah to rest as the Chronicler meant him to be remembered — a king honoured living and dead, whose reforming zeal, whatever the coldness of his people, was written on their consciences even as they buried him, and whose son Manasseh now took a throne his father had held in faith.
